content:
Tracking electron recoils underground

The XENONnT experiment operates at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory in Italy. Situated under 1,400 meters of rock, the shield naturally blocks everyday cosmic radiation from disturbing sensitive instruments.

Inside its central time projection chamber, the detector holds nearly six metric tons of purified liquid xenon. When a solar neutrino strikes an electron in the target, the interaction triggers a subtle flash of light and charge.

Researchers analyzed data gathered across two science runs totaling over two ton-years of exposure. Their equipment detected particle interactions at energies down to 17 kiloelectronvolts, expanding low-energy detection capabilities.

Measuring neutrinos from solar fusion

The Sun generates energy through nuclear fusion reactions occurring constantly within its core. This fusion process converts hydrogen into helium while releasing streams of low-energy neutrinos into space.

Most of these particles originate from the primary proton-proton fusion chain. The XENONnT team successfully measured this primary solar flux by tracking direct electron-scattering events inside the liquid target.

The team measured the signal at a five-sigma confidence level. This result indicates a real signal above background noise, though the calculation relies on specific assumptions.

Controlling background noise in the detector

Solar neutrino signals are faint and easily obscured by trace radioactivity inside detector components. Managing ambient background radiation remained the central technical challenge for the research team throughout operations.

Engineers carefully screened every structural material and used continuous cryogenic distillation to remove radioactive radon. They also modeled potential interference from surrounding metal components, lead isotopes, and ambient gamma rays.

Filtering these background signals allowed the team to isolate rare particle collisions with confidence. Without extreme shielding and active distillation, local radiation would easily swamp the faint solar readings.

Distinguishing neutrinos from dark matter

Neutrinos possess tiny masses, carry no electric charge, and interact rarely with ordinary matter. However, astrophysicists have established that ordinary neutrinos cannot account for the universe’s missing dark matter.

Because neutrinos traveled near the speed of light during early cosmic epochs, they could not form stable galaxies. They contribute a small fraction of total mass rather than driving large-scale structure formation.

The XENONnT result focuses strictly on measuring solar particle fluxes rather than detecting dark matter. The measurement demonstrates new detector versatility without claiming the discovery of exotic particles.

Expanding the search at Gran Sasso

This detection extends a long tradition of solar neutrino research conducted at the Gran Sasso facility. Earlier experiments like Borexino measured low-energy solar neutrinos using liquid organic scintillators at higher thresholds.

XENONnT reaches lower energy ranges by utilizing a massive liquid xenon target. The detector also recently recorded a separate interaction type where higher-energy neutrinos bounce directly off atomic nuclei.

Future analyses will focus on refining background noise models and collecting additional observational data. Combining multiple interaction channels will give scientists clearer insights into core solar processes.

What remains uncertain

The XENONnT measurement confirms that dark matter detectors can successfully gather low-energy solar neutrino data. However, the result does not reveal new fundamental forces or explain dark matter.

The research paper remains an unreviewed preprint awaiting formal evaluation by academic peers. Independent experts must still audit the team’s background modeling and signal extraction methods before publication.

Source: XENON Collaboration, “First Measurement of Solar Neutrinos through Elastic Neutrino-Electron Scattering at the keV Scale,” arXiv preprint, 2026.
